title: A Sensor That Lies Like the Real One: Bias, Noise, Steps, Delay and Dropouts, in the Order They Happen

questions.question: Why is a perfect simulated sensor dangerous?
options: A controller tested on it has never met a delay, noise or a step size: one that overshot by 0.19 with it overshot by 0.65 with a sensor 60 ms old
questions.explanation: It is the one fake that is always wrong.

questions.question: In what order does the model apply a sensor's faults?
options: Truth plus bias plus noise, then the range, then the resolution, then the delay, and last the chance of the whole reading being lost
questions.explanation: The order is the order they happen in a real sensor.

questions.question: A resolution of 0.1 gave an rms error of 0.02885. What predicts that?
options: The step over the square root of twelve, 0.02887: the quantization error

questions.question: A reading is lost. What should the model give?
options: A reading marked invalid that carries the last good value, so a loop that ignores the mark does not jump to the origin
questions.explanation: 2052 of 20000 were lost at a chance of 0.1.

questions.question: Why does every reading draw its random numbers whatever the options?
options: So that switching one effect on does not change what another does: the delayed sensor read exactly what the plain one had read two samples before
questions.explanation: Otherwise adding a delay to a test would change its noise.

questions.question: The noise and coarse steps added almost nothing to the overshoot in the last test. What does that say?
options: That for this controller the delay is what matters, and the way to find out which effects matter is to switch them on one at a time
